The first NVIDIA DGX Station-class system to cross our collective desk is Gigabyte’s W775-V10-L01, with Gigabyte taking the task of building a desk-side GB300-based system quite seriously. That may sound simple in concept, but in practice, the system is far beyond what you might expect. It is liquid-cooled, and with a 1.6kW maximum power draw, it can run on even most 120V circuits. We tested the ConnectX-8 400Gbps RDMA networking and found something we did not expect. We even tested the high-speed C2C link between the NVIDIA Grace 72-core CPU and the NVIDIA “Blackwell Ultra” (B300) GPU. We have been working on this article for some time, and it is just a wild machine.

The W775 throws a lot of hardware at the user, and this is the crux of what makes DGX Station systems compelling. It is not just a Grace CPU or just a server-grade, HBM3E-equipped Blackwell Ultra GPU, or even a high-end dual 400Gbps ConnectX-8 network interface card. Instead, it is a combination of all of this hardware and more, all of the critical components of a GB300 server, brought down to a desktop workstation. Even calling it a GB300 server in a tower undersells the idea a bit, but it gets the concept across well enough. This is not a slice of the Grace Blackwell ecosystem like GB10-based Spark boxes, but it is the complete and unrestrained Grace Blackwell experience.

Gigabyte loaned us this unit so we could make this content. We have to say this is sponsored.

## Gigabyte W775-V10-L01 External Hardware Overview

Thanks to the combination of some very large chips inside as well as an extensive liquid cooling system, Gigabyte’s W775-V10-L01 resides in a full-size PC tower case measuring 50cm tall and 53cm deep. But more than the size, if you try to lift it, you will quickly feel the weight of the system and the liquid cooling system inside, which brings the system to a hefty 29kg (about 64 lbs). It is heavy enough that Gigabyte strongly advises using two people to move the system (team lifting), and even specifies where each person should place their hands in order to avoid lifting the system by its plastic front panel (which cannot support the weight of the system).

With that said, the W775 is otherwise a fairly unassuming system given that this is a hundred-thousand-dollar workstation. The case itself is a pretty typical PC chassis with only minimal customization for the hardware inside. So this is not a heavily customized design ala DGX Spark systems, and the ability to use standard PC cases is one of the few aspects of DGX Station systems that OEMs are given any liberty to customize. With that said, Gigabyte does seem to be using a unique design here for the W775, as we have not been able to find any other Gigabyte systems with a matching case.

Surprisingly, the front of the W775’s case is merely decorative, rather than serving any cooling function. Gigabyte is not using the front of the system as an airflow intake (as we see on most full tower systems), and instead they are making extensive use of every other side of the case as either an intake or exhaust. This does help with acoustics some, as it means there are not any fans directly facing forward towards the user.

On the left side of the case we find a vent cutout covering a couple of fans to serve as an intake.

Meanwhile, on the right side of the case, we catch the back side of a radiator, with three fans pushing air through it as part of the system’s extensive liquid cooling system.

This also means that there are no I/O ports or buttons on the front of the case. Given the size, weight, and the amount of heat this system puts out, Gigabyte intends for the W775 to be a floor computer, so its ports and controls have been configured accordingly, placing them along the top side of the case.

For all of the W775’s I/O capabilities, the top panel I/O is actually a bit spartan. Here we find a pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports and a single 10Gbps USB-C port towards the far end. You will not find any USB4-speed ports on the system. Any transfers faster than 10Gbps will need to go through the system’s massive throughput 400Gb QSFP112s via the integrated ConnectX-8 SuperNIC. Actually, the 10GbE NIC also goes through the ConnectX-8 as well.

While this is absolutely nitpicking on our part, for the price of the system it is surprising to see that Gigabyte has not bothered to use any kind of official (and suggested) USB-IF logos to identify the USB ports. Especially as they have opted not to use blue plastic here for the USB-A ports, there is nothing to indicate that these are USB 3.x ports.

In any case, along with the trio of USB ports, the top of the system also includes discrete headphones-out and mic-in jacks for audio, saving a trip to the back of the heavy system.

Speaking of the rear of the system, here is a look at that. Since this is a (largely) standard PC chassis, we see the familiar fan, rear I/O, expansion slot, and PSU layout of the ATX form factor. The chassis can accept either a 120mm or 140mm fan for the rear exhaust, with Gigabyte opting for a 120mm Sunon fan.

For the rear I/O, the system is dominated by networking. Including the 1GbE port for the BMC, there are four different Ethernet ports on the W775, which are routed to three different controllers.

Chief among these are the two QSFP112 ports, which are fed by NVIDIA’s powerful ConnectX-8 “SuperNIC”. Each port offers 400Gbps networking, and like the QSFP ports on the DGX Spark, these are the primary means by which the system is meant to network with high-speed storage and/or other DGX Station-based systems. The ConnectX-8 SuperNIC driving these ports does a lot of heavy lifting beyond networking, and the capabilities and limitations of these QSFP ports are somewhat complex as a result. We will get into that more when we talk about the system topology.

We tried both QSFP112 DACs and optics in here. Something I will point out is that there is not a ton of airflow around the optical cages, so the NVIDIA MMS1X00-N5400 QSFP112 optics at around 10W ended up working well for us. These cost a bit more, but in the data center tours we do, the data center tech tend to tell us that NVIDIA’s optics work better than some low-cost brands when installed in hot aisles.

For more mundane networking use cases, the system also has a pair of RJ45 Ethernet jacks. The left port, labeled ‘M’, connects to the BMC and is for system management. Management is handled by OpenBMC with a HTML5 iKVM and everything, but since this is an enormous review, we are not going too deep into that. The RJ45 jack on the right side is a 10Gb Ethernet port powered by Marvell’s tried-and-true AQC113C controller. The topology of this system is fascinating, so the AQC113C actually is attached to the ConnectX-8 SuperNIC, not the CPU directly.

Below are the rest of the W775’s USB ports. These four ports all run at 10Gbps, matching the speed of the USB-C port on the top of the system. Unlike the top USB-A ports, Gigabyte (or rather, NVIDIA) used blue plastic here to indicate these are high-speed ports. That said, Gigabyte’s block diagram indicates these ports route through a hub, so you shouldn’t expect to get 10Gbps out of each one simultaneously.

To the right of that, we have a trio of audio jacks, all powered by a Realtek ALC4080 audio codec.

At the end of the rear I/O panel, we have two more ports that are tied to the BMC. On the left is a serial UART in a micro-USB form factor. To the right is a Mini DisplayPort output from the BMC for system management and configuration. DGX Station systems do not have a true integrated display GPU within them (Blackwell Ultra is more of a compute accelerator), so the BMC is the only graphics output out of the box. For a full-featured graphics solution, DGX Station systems can be paired with an NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell video card.

Briefly, we also find a pair of plugs here. While the W775 does not come with a wireless radio installed, the chassis and motherboard can fully support one if desired; in that case, these plugs are used for the antenna leads.

Finally, here is a look at the bottom of the system, where the power supply resides. Thanks in large part to the GB300 accelerator inside each of them, DGX Station systems are extremely power-hungry, and NVIDIA is right at the limit for a single North American power outlet here with their 1600 Watt power supply. The 80 PLUS Platinum-rated PSU requires a high-capacity C19 power cable to safely handle that amperage, and requires a 20-amp circuit to drive it. In practice, this system effectively requires its own dedicated 20A circuit.

As an aside, while you can just barely see it, the PSU is home to yet another fan on the system, pulling in cold air from beneath the system to cool the PSU. As a result, every side except the front side of the system is some kind of air intake or exhaust.

That is the outside of Gigabyte’s W775 DGX Station. For the rest of the story, let us dive into the system’s chassis, where this gets very different.

Calling AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ chips well-received in the mini-PC market is probably an understatement. The high-performance Zen 5 chips have proven particularly adept in this market thanks to a combination of CPU and iGPU performance, plus high memory capacity and bandwidth from LPDDR5X. Especially in this era of AI development, software developers looking to test and run inference locally have been quick to snap up the mini-PCs.

One result of this popularity is that AMD’s many mini-PC partners have been addressing a market large enough (and with margins big enough) to justify working through multiple generations of mini-PC designs within the Ryzen AI Max family’s lifecycle. A prime example is GMtec, one of the industry’s better-known mini-PC vendors. Last year the company released its first Ryzen AI Max+ box with the EVO-X2 , and this year they are back again with a new and very different Ryzen AI Max+ mini-PC design that they are dubbing the EVO-X3.

The EVO-X3 stands out in a crowded mini-PC market for a few reasons. First and foremost, the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 SoC at the heart of the system delivers its AI performance and enables it to tap into 128GB of LPDDR5X memory for its iGPU. The second, and far more unique reason is its connectivity. GMKtec has outfitted the system with an OCuLink port, making it a rare Ryzen AI Max system with external PCIe connectivity, and it surpasses even Thunderbolt 4 systems in available bandwidth.

Surprisingly, GMKtec is aiming the EVO-X3 at a pretty broad customer base, even pitching the OCuLink port as a gaming feature for use with an eGPU. In practice, though, it is hard to imagine the system being used as anything other than a productivity desktop, especially since GMKtec even preloads the system with AI development software. That is okay, because the Ryzen AI Max platform has proven well suited for that role.

## GMKtec EVO-X3 External hardware Overview

One of the most notable design aspects of the previous iteration, the EVO-X2 mini-PC, was that the system operates upright, a pretty big distinction from the more classic wide-and-low desktop mini-PC form factors. For the EVO-X3, GMKtec seems to have doubled down on this design strategy even more, resulting in a mini-PC that can only be described as a metal monolith. The stange form factor makes more sense once we get inside.

The metal, by the way, is a notable change from the EVO-X2, which notably (and noticeably) featured a plastic chassis. On the other hand, this EVO-X3 is fully metal. The overall monolithic design is even more clearly meant to stand, especially with the (required) base attached.

The tall, slim profile does mean that there is very little to the front of the system, though. For the purposes of our article layout (and your browser window), we have laid the mini-PC flat, which goes to show just how thin the 41mm PC is. Despite packing in a high-performance processor, it is not much thicker than a desktop replacement-class workstation laptop.

This view also underscores the limited I/O connectivity on the front of the PC, however. Aside from the 3.5mm combo audio jack, GMKtec has placed only two USB-A ports on the front of the system, and only one is a fast 5Gbps USB 3.x port. The second USB-A port is an even slower USB 2.x port, and there is no front-panel USB Type-C connectivity. The system supports plenty of I/O bandwidth, as we will see, but just not in the front.

Meanwhile, towards the other end of the system, we find a rather striking neon green power button sitting within the grey metal chassis.

Speaking of aesthetics, the EVO-X3’s standing design is not just a style choice for GMKtec. Both the left and right sizes feature significant ventilation. Meanwhile, if there is any doubt about what the primary market is for this system, the “AI workstation” labeling etched into the left side of the case should remove all doubt.

Shifting to the rear of the system, we find much better ventilation with clearly visible heatsinks. More importantly, this is also where the rest of the system’s I/O lives, including its unusual OCuLink port.

Starting there, GMKtec has opted to route four of the Ryzen SoC’s PCIe lanes to an OCuLink port for directly attaching a device to the system. This port can technically connect any device, but the most common use for OCuLink these days is attaching a dock for an external GPU, making it possible to add a high-end video card (or other accelerator) to the system. The OCuLink specification itself tops out at PCIe Gen4 x4 (or ~64Gbps), so it is not comparable to the amount of bandwidth a full-fledged PCIe slot can offer. With the Ryzen AI Max chips offering only 16 PCIe lanes to begin with (all PCIe Gen4), GMKtec can realistically offer only 4 lanes, since they need the other lanes for other features.

In any case, the drawback to OCuLink as an external port is the same here as it always was: it is not a hot-plug-capable port. That is why GMKtec has put a very explicit sticker here warning users not to plug (or unplug) an OCuLink cable while the system is operating. On that note, credit to the engineer who had the foresight here to put the OCuLink port to the left of the DC power jack, isolating it from the hotplug-capable USB ports.

The thin profile of the EVO-X3 means that GMKtec is relying on an external power supply here. At 230 Watts, they technically could have gotten away with a USB-C power supply, but barrel jack units are still a common fixture here.

Next is the system’s sole USB-C port. A native feature of the Ryzen AI Max SoC, this is a full 40Gbps USB4 port that also supports DP Alt Mode to double as a display output for the system. In fact, this is the only way to get DisplayPort video out of the X3, as there is also no dedicated DisplayPort output on the system. Otherwise, given GMKtec’s focus on external I/O bandwidth with the X3, it is somewhat surprising to see that they did not include a second 40Gbps USB-C port, as the Ryzen SoC provides for two ports.

To the right, we have the system’s sole dedicated display output: an HDMI 2.1 port. Another native feature of the Ryzen AI Max SoC, there is little reason not to include it here.

Moving down the line, we find another USB Type-A port. The second (and final) USB port on the rear of the system is a 10Gbps port. Including the earlier Type-C port, this gives the X3 a total of 4 USB ports, which is serviceable, but it falls short compared to most other Ryzen AI Max mini-PCs that offer a few more ports. In practice, it means the OCuLink port and USB-C port are doing a lot of heavy lifting as far as I/O goes, as there simply are not a lot of ports otherwise for plugging in peripherals after you add a mouse and keyboard. There is again a reason for this that we will see inside.

Finally, we have the system’s dedicated Ethernet jack. This is a 2.5GbE port backed by Realtek’s RTL8125BG controller. This is a common enough sight across PCs these days, but for a recently-released Ryzen AI Max system, it is a shame that GMKtec did not use one of Realtek’s newer 10GbE chips, which have become readily available (and relatively cheap) this year. Not including 10GbE is quickly becoming a missed opportunity for AI development-focused PC.

Shifting perspectives once again, here is a shot of what is on top of the X3 when the system is standing. Matching the colorful neon green accent of the power button we saw earlier, the solid green top gives the system a distinct two-tone color scheme. And perhaps a smidge of irony for the Ryzen-powered system, since it is much closer to NVIDIA’s shade of green than AMD’s.

In any case, the top features another airflow vent as well. So, like virtually every other side of the system, it needs to be kept clear for cooling purposes. This also serves as the one significant non-metallic portion of the system for cleanly routing the wireless radio antennas.

Last but not least, here is a look at the bottom of the system. Normally hidden by the system’s base, this is where GMKtec has placed the product stickers, as well as the means to access the system’s internals.

Looking at the base itself, interestingly, GMKtec has opted to etch the full system information into the base, including its power specifications and regulatory trademarks. This ensures that the information is visible without dismantling the system, but it means that the base is an integral part of the system for more than just holding up the monolithic mini-PC.

The base relies on a pair of screws to secure it to the bottom of the mini-PC’s chassis. GMKtec has also taken care to include rubber feet on the base to prevent slippage. Unfortunately, these feet are not built into the base, and in fact have to be removed to access the screws that hold the base on. Which means this is not a design that is meant to be opened more than a couple of times, as it will wear out the adhesive on the feet.

Now that we have taken a look at the outside of the EVO-X3, let us dig into the guts of the system.
